quote: What do you need to information?
stewart_read: This is the customer's first comprehension-friction signal on the open-ended interest question, and it recurs at 01:52 with an explicit 'I don't understand.' The rep's response ('Just trying to get the information?') doesn't simplify or confirm understanding, it just restates intent.
alternative_hypothesis: Some of this could be an audio/transcription artifact rather than genuine language friction, given the transcript's own speaker-misattribution issues (e.g., 01:27 'rep: Yes.').
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to slow down and check for understanding explicitly ('does that question make sense?') the first time a customer gives an off-target answer, rather than plowing through the checklist.

quote: I use 13,000 kilowatt hours per year.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers a specific, usable usage figure unprompted. The rep files it ('Perfect. That that will help a lot.') as design input but never reflects it back as leverage or ties it to bill pain later in the call.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to treat volunteered usage numbers as a hook — e.g., acknowledge the number specifically and connect it to what the closer will show, rather than only logging it for the design team.

stewart_read: Customer gives a bill figure at 01:42 ('$200'), which the rep immediately reacts to at 01:44 ('per month. Oh, okay. Wow.'). The rep captures the number and shows verbal surprise but pivots straight into the tax-credit qualifier rather than using the number to build urgency or align against the utility.
coaching_implication: This is a capture-without-flip pattern — the rep should be coached to hold on the bill number a beat longer, e.g. tie it explicitly to what solar could offset, before moving to qualifiers.

stewart_read: Customer's first ask for a written proposal instead of a call. Rep redirects to a phone call, correctly holding the hard rule against sending numbers before the specialist call, but the reassurance is generic ('typically, at our company, we just do...') rather than addressing why the customer wants it in writing.
coaching_implication: Rep held the correct policy; the gap is reassurance depth, not policy adherence. Coach the rep to acknowledge the underlying want (wanting to see real numbers, not just verbal) before redirecting to the phone-call format.

quote: I need to I need to know your price and your sentence.
stewart_read: Second occurrence of the same request. Rep repeats the same structural answer ('that's what we'll go over in the phone call') without varying the reassurance or acknowledging this is the customer's second ask.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to notice repetition from the customer and escalate the reassurance (e.g., name a concrete element that will be covered) rather than reusing the same line verbatim.

quote: The tomorrow, this is price and sentence.
stewart_read: Third occurrence of the same pricing-in-writing concern. Rep's response ('I'll make sure we we show that show you that right away so we won't waste your time') is the strongest of the three but comes only after two prior identical asks were met with unchanged phrasing.
coaching_implication: This 3x repetition on the same unresolved concern is the clearest coaching signal on the call — the manager should walk the rep through varying reassurance across repeated asks instead of running the same script line three times.

quote: But I do know we have some availability tomorrow and Thursday.
stewart_read: The call ends at 05:01 mid-sentence with no recap of the appointment, no one-hour block mention, no no-driving/computer instruction, and no explicit 'is that fair?' handshake — just a truncated thank-you.
alternative_hypothesis: The transcript could be cut off before the button-up was completed off-recording, but nothing in the available text shows it happening.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep on always running the full button-up (recap day/time, hour block, no-driving expectation, text confirmation) verbally before the call ends, regardless of how the conversation naturally winds down.

quote: Okay. Awesome. Is it just a asphalt shingle roof?
stewart_read: Customer volunteers his roof is only 5 years old at 01:02 ('I mean, five years old'), a positive qualification signal (no re-roof barrier), but the rep doesn't acknowledge this as good news beyond a generic 'Okay. Awesome.'
coaching_implication: Minor, but coach the rep to briefly flag positive qualification signals like roof age back to the customer ('great, that means no roofing concerns at all') to build a small confidence moment in the call.
